meaning: Talking quickly and continuously in a silly or confusing way; also the soft sound of flowing water
trick: BAB-BAB-BAB — a baby making the same sounds again and again.
examples: The baby was babbling happily in her cot.
We sat by the babbling stream.

usage.pattern: someone is babbling (on) about something; a babbling brook/stream

meaning: The lowest, deepest sound in music; a guitar or voice that makes this sound (pronounced like 'base')
trick: Bass is the BASE (bottom) of the music — and it sounds like 'base'.
examples: Turn down the bass, the walls are shaking.
He plays bass guitar in a band.

usage.pattern: play (the) bass; the bass (sound) in something

meaning: Completely crazy (rude slang, often 'batshit crazy')
trick: Bats fly around wildly in the dark — total madness.
examples: That plan is batshit crazy.
He went batshit when he saw the bill.

usage.pattern: someone/something is batshit (crazy); go batshit

meaning: Slightly crazy or strange (informal, mild)
trick: 'Bats in the belfry' — a head full of bats is a bit batty.
examples: My batty old uncle talks to his plants.
The noise is driving me batty.

usage.pattern: someone is a bit batty; something drives someone batty

meaning: A huge, uncountable number (informal, made-up number)
trick: Bigger than a billion — a BAZILLION!
examples: I have a bazillion things to do today.
She has asked me that question a bazillion times.

usage.pattern: a bazillion things/times; bazillions of something

meaning: Signalling someone to come closer, usually with a hand; looking inviting
trick: BECKON ≈ 'back on' — waving your hand to say 'come back here'.
examples: The teacher was beckoning me to come to her desk.
The cool water looked beckoning on a hot day.

usage.pattern: beckon (to) someone to do something; beckon someone over

meaning: Too ill or weak to get out of bed
trick: BED + RIDDEN — 'ridden' (stuck) to the bed.
examples: Grandpa was bedridden for a week with the flu.
After the accident, she was bedridden for months.

usage.pattern: be/become bedridden (with an illness / for a time)

meaning: A pale, light brown colour, like sand
trick: BEIGE rhymes with 'page' — the colour of an old paper page.
examples: She bought a beige sofa for the living room.
The walls were painted a plain beige.

usage.pattern: a beige something; something is beige; painted beige

meaning: A graph shaped like a bell, showing that most results are in the middle and few are very high or very low
trick: Draw it and it looks like a BELL — tall in the middle, low at the ends.
examples: Most students' marks fell in the middle of the bell curve.
Heights of people follow a bell curve.

usage.pattern: follow a bell curve; on/in the bell curve; grade on a bell curve

meaning: Helpful, useful or good for you
trick: BENE = good (like 'benefit') — something that does you good.
examples: Exercise is beneficial for your health.
The extra class was beneficial to everyone.

usage.pattern: something is beneficial for/to someone/something

meaning: Advantages or good results from something; also money or help given by a company or government
trick: BENE = good + FIT — things that fit in well and do good.
examples: One of the benefits of walking is better sleep.
The job comes with health benefits.

usage.pattern: the benefits of something/doing; something benefits someone; benefit from something

meaning: Gentle and kind; (of an illness or lump) not harmful or dangerous
trick: BENIGN ≈ 'be nice' — harmless and gentle. Opposite: malignant.
examples: The doctor said the lump was benign.
He gave a benign smile to the children.

usage.pattern: something is benign; a benign tumour/smile

meaning: Gave something as an honour, gift or reward
trick: BE-STOWED — the king STOWED (placed) a gift in your hands.
examples: The award was bestowed on the best student.
The king bestowed a medal on the brave soldier.

usage.pattern: bestow something on/upon someone

meaning: Very confused and unable to understand what is happening
trick: BE-WILD-ered — lost in the wild, not knowing which way to go.
examples: He looked bewildered by the long question.
The tourists were bewildered in the busy station.

usage.pattern: be bewildered by/at something; look bewildered

meaning: An important or powerful person (informal)
trick: In the old days, important men wore BIG WIGs.
examples: Some company bigwigs visited our office.
He acts like a bigwig, but he's just a clerk.

usage.pattern: a bigwig in/at something (a company, politics)

meaning: Folders with rings or clips for holding loose papers together
trick: They BIND your papers together.
examples: Keep your notes in these binders.
She has three binders full of recipes.

usage.pattern: put/keep something in binders

meaning: Very strange or unusual
trick: BIZARRE sounds like 'bazaar' — a crowded market full of strange things.
examples: I had a bizarre dream last night.
It was bizarre to see snow in summer.

usage.pattern: something is bizarre; it is bizarre that ...

meaning: Done openly and obviously, without any shame (usually something bad)
trick: BLATANT ≈ 'blast it out' — done loudly, for everyone to see.
examples: That was a blatant lie.
He made a blatant mistake in front of everyone.

usage.pattern: a blatant lie/mistake/example of something

meaning: A large, strong fire; or a very bright light
trick: BLAZE ≈ 'blast of flames'.
examples: Firefighters put out the blaze quickly.
The garden was a blaze of colour in spring.

usage.pattern: a blaze (fire); something blazes; a blaze of colour/light

meaning: So bright or strong that you cannot see properly
trick: It makes you BLIND for a moment.
examples: The sun was blinding when we came out.
There was a blinding flash of light.

usage.pattern: a blinding light/flash; something is blinding

meaning: Window coverings that can be pulled down or turned to block light
trick: They make the window BLIND — no light gets in.
examples: Please close the blinds, the sun is too bright.
She opened the blinds to let the light in.

usage.pattern: open/close/pull down the blinds

meaning: Swollen and too full, often from eating too much or from gas
trick: Like a BOAT puffed up with air — BLOATED.
examples: I felt bloated after the big lunch.
The company has a bloated budget.

usage.pattern: feel bloated (after something); a bloated budget/system

meaning: Produced flowers; or grew and developed in a good way
trick: BLOSSOM = flower — something that bloomed like a flower.
examples: The cherry trees blossomed in April.
She blossomed into a confident speaker.

usage.pattern: something blossomed; someone blossomed into something

meaning: A big party or celebration; an easy, one-sided win; or a sudden burst tyre
trick: Everything BLOWS OUT — a huge party, a huge win, or a tyre that bursts.
examples: They had a blowout party for her birthday.
Our team won the match in a blowout, 6–0.

usage.pattern: have a blowout (party); win in a blowout; a tyre blowout

meaning: Loud, aggressive or proud talk with little effect; (of wind) to blow in strong gusts
trick: BLUSTER ≈ 'blow + bluff' — lots of wind and noise, nothing real.
examples: Ignore his bluster; he won't really do anything.
The wind blustered all night.

usage.pattern: someone's bluster; someone blusters (about something); the wind blusters

meaning: A very large amount (informal)
trick: Enough to fill a whole BOAT.
examples: He made a boatload of money.
We have a boatload of homework this week.

usage.pattern: a boatload of something

meaning: Fake, false or not genuine
trick: BOGUS ≈ 'bogey' — a scary fake thing that isn't real.
examples: The email was a bogus offer.
He showed a bogus ID card.

usage.pattern: a bogus something; something is bogus

meaning: Attacked continuously; or given too many questions, messages or things at once
trick: Like being hit by BOMBs again and again.
examples: The singer was bombarded with questions.
My phone was bombarded with messages.

usage.pattern: be bombarded with something; bombard someone with something

meaning: Very close to a limit; only just acceptable or not
trick: Standing right on the BORDER LINE — not clearly on either side.
examples: His marks were borderline for passing.
That joke was borderline rude.

usage.pattern: something is borderline (rude/pass); on the borderline of something

meaning: (Slang, joking) Ideas or facts so interesting they excite your mind
trick: Something that gets your BRAIN really excited.
examples: Space facts give me brain boners.
That science video was full of brain boners.

usage.pattern: something gives someone brain boners

meaning: Breaking a rule, law or promise; or a gap or break in a wall or defence
trick: BREACH ≈ BREAK — both start with BRE.
examples: Sharing the password was a breach of the rules.
Water came through a breach in the wall.

usage.pattern: a breach of something (rules/contract/trust); breach a rule/wall

meaning: Raised animals or plants to produce young ones (past of 'breed'); also, brought up
trick: BRED = past of BREED — 'born and bred'.
examples: He was born and bred in Mumbai.
These dogs were bred to guard sheep.

usage.pattern: be bred for/to do something; born and bred (in a place)

meaning: Types of animals within a species; or produces young ones or causes something
trick: Dog BREEDS — Labrador, Pug, Beagle.
examples: There are many breeds of dogs.
Laziness breeds more laziness.

usage.pattern: breeds of something; something breeds something (causes it)

meaning: The edge of a steep place; the point just before something happens ('on the brink of')
trick: BRINK ≈ BRIM — right at the edge, about to spill over.
examples: The company was on the brink of closing.
She stood at the brink of the cliff.

usage.pattern: be on the brink of something / of doing something

meaning: Having a dark mark on the skin from being hit; also emotionally hurt
trick: BRUISE — the blue-purple mark after a bump.
examples: He bruised his knee when he fell.
She felt bruised after the argument.

usage.pattern: bruise your knee/arm; feel bruised (emotionally)

meaning: The main force or worst part of something bad ('bear the brunt of')
trick: BRUNT ≈ 'brunt = blunt hit' — you take the hardest hit.
examples: The coastal towns bore the brunt of the storm.
I took the brunt of the blame.

usage.pattern: bear/take the brunt of something

meaning: Annoying or bothering someone again and again (informal)
trick: Like a BUG buzzing around your head — it keeps bugging you.
examples: Stop bugging me while I'm working!
Something has been bugging me all day.

usage.pattern: something is bugging someone; stop bugging someone (about something)

meaning: (Informal) A homeless or lazy person; the buttocks (British); 'bummed' means sad
trick: A BUM just sits on his BUM all day.
examples: Don't be a lazy bum, get up and help!
He fell on his bum on the ice.

usage.pattern: a lazy bum; on your bum; bum something off someone (borrow)

meaning: Mexican food: a soft flour tortilla rolled around a filling like beans, rice and meat
trick: BURRITO = 'little donkey' in Spanish — it carries all the filling.
examples: We had burritos for dinner.
She ordered two chicken burritos.

usage.pattern: have/order/make burritos

meaning: A low humming sound like a bee; or a feeling of excitement
trick: The sound a bee makes — bzzzz!
examples: I heard the buzz of a bee near the window.
There was a buzz of excitement in the room.

usage.pattern: the buzz of something; a buzz of excitement; something buzzes
